provenance.note: Generated by drivers/regression on the pystatsval harness against a PyPI-installed pystatistics==4.3.2. This is the clean re-validation of the 4.3.x line. 4.3.0 added prior weights (weights=) and an offset term (offset=) to fit() and fixed the Gamma AIC; 4.3.1 made the negative-binomial AIC/BIC count the estimated theta and exposed theta via result.info['theta']; 4.3.2 fixed three correctness defects that re-validating 4.3.1 surfaced -- (1) GPU OLS standard errors no longer understate on ill-conditioned designs (a 4.3.0 regression where the covariance was inverted from a float32 Gram; now computed in float64), (2) Gamma/Gaussian BIC now penalize the estimated dispersion with log(n) (was the AIC constant 2), and (3) the binomial deviance/AIC/BIC clamp fitted probabilities at machine epsilon like R (was 1e-10). All three are validated here. Hosts: powerhouse (Apple Silicon, CPU fp64 + Metal/MPS fp32, R 4.5.2, Apple Accelerate BLAS) and forge (NVIDIA CUDA, CPU fp64 + CUDA fp32/fp64, R 4.3.3, reference netlib BLAS).
provenance.baseline: Compare against reports/regression-v4.2.4.md. Correctness, CPU-vs-R speed, GPU scaling, R10/R11/R12 and the inference SE/CI proof are re-measured at 4.3.2. New at 4.3.x: weights=/offset= are validated as correctness (R10, previously a fail-loud gap), and AIC/BIC vs R plus negbin theta vs MASS::glm.nb are now checked. The 4.3.1 GPU-OLS-SE inference-silent-wrong regression caught by the inference_se study is fixed in 4.3.2 (inference_se now reports zero silent-wrong on both MPS and CUDA).

reference.name: R stats::lm / stats::glm / MASS::glm.nb
reference.what: R's lm() (OLS via pivoted QR) and glm() (GLM via IRLS), plus MASS::glm.nb() for the negative binomial. pystatistics unifies lm and glm, so the head-to-head pulls from both. Ridge is cross-checked against MASS::lm.ridge / glmnet in the drivers.

studies.title: Correctness vs R — Powerhouse (Apple Silicon, CPU / fp64)
studies.note: CPU OLS + 5 GLM families vs R on real datasets. Coefficients match R to round-off (~1e-11..1e-15; negbin coef ~1e-4 and gamma/poisson SEs ~1e-3..1e-8 are the documented dispersion/theta tolerances). As of 4.2.2 the CPU fit also MEETS/BEATS R on wall-clock (speedup_vs_r 1.4-2.8x here) -- the Prime-Directive parity requirement. As of 4.3.x the information criteria are validated too: AIC and BIC agree with R to round-off across the families (Gamma AIC/BIC fixed in 4.3.0/4.3.2; negbin AIC/BIC counting theta in 4.3.1; binomial deviance/AIC/BIC clamp fixed in 4.3.2), and the negative-binomial auto-estimated theta (exposed via result.info['theta'] since 4.3.1) matches MASS::glm.nb.

studies.title: Correctness vs R — Forge (Linux x86-64, CPU / fp64)
studies.note: Second-host CPU-vs-R correctness (Forge, R 4.3.3): identical round-off agreement; CPU speedup_vs_r 2.2-5x (CPU beats R). As of 4.3.x the information criteria are validated too: AIC and BIC agree with R to round-off across the families (Gamma AIC/BIC fixed in 4.3.0/4.3.2; negbin AIC/BIC counting theta in 4.3.1; binomial deviance/AIC/BIC clamp fixed in 4.3.2), and the negative-binomial auto-estimated theta (exposed via result.info['theta'] since 4.3.1) matches MASS::glm.nb.

studies.title: CPU vs R across problem sizes — Powerhouse (priority 3: CPU must never lag R)
studies.note: The first-class CPU-speed deliverable (RIGOR priority 3 / R1): the CPU path is the R-equivalent path and must NEVER lag R. Wall-clock for pystatistics CPU vs R across n from 50 (where fixed Python-dispatch overhead bites hardest) to 500k, for OLS and every GLM family (negbin capped at 1e4 -- glm.nb theta-profiling is slow), p=8. Both sides timed as the full user-facing call (pystatistics fit(X,y) building its design; R lm/glm/glm.nb from a formula building the model matrix), averaged over many repeats so small-n fits are resolved. Result: pystatistics CPU MEETS-OR-BEATS R at EVERY size and family -- speedup_vs_r >= 1.3x throughout, including the small-n regime (n=50: OLS 9.8x, GLMs 1.5-2.6x), so pystat_lags_r is false for all 28 points. Host R links Apple Accelerate (a fast vendor BLAS), so this is the honest test, not a slow-BLAS flatter. Per the slopes study the empirical complexity classes match (both ~O(n) at fixed p); there is no complexity-class gap (R1).

studies.title: CPU vs R empirical complexity (log-log slope of wall vs n) — Powerhouse
studies.note: Empirical complexity exponent (slope of log10 wall vs log10 n, fitted over n>=1000 to skip the fixed-overhead floor) for each engine. pystatistics and R land in the SAME complexity class for every family (~O(n) at fixed p; slopes ~0.8-0.95), so pystatistics' CPU lead is a constant-factor win, not a slope that will reverse at larger n -- the R1 complexity-class check passes.

studies.title: Device scaling — Powerhouse: CPU (fp64) vs MPS (fp32)
studies.note: GPU value proposition (vs the priority-3 CPU-vs-R claim above): the GPU path trades double precision for float32, so it has to BUY SPEED over the CPU to be worth using at all -- a slower-and-less-accurate GPU would be pointless. This table shows the MPS GPU earns its place where it is meant to be used: at large n with a non-trivial p it is materially faster than the fp64 CPU (up to ~18x for OLS and ~10x for the GLM families at n=5e5, p=128). The advantage shrinks toward parity for narrow designs (p=8) or small n, where fixed dispatch/transfer overhead dominates and the CPU is the better choice -- that envelope is reported honestly rather than hidden. The CPU remains the reference/accuracy path (priority 3 owns the R-equivalent claim); the GPU is the throughput path and is held to actually delivering throughput. OLS + GLM device scaling, CPU (fp64) vs MPS (fp32); as of 4.2.4 the MPS float32 GLM inner solve is a gated matrix-free conjugate gradient (squaring-free), convergence/timing matching 4.2.3.

studies.title: Device scaling — Forge: CPU (fp64) vs CUDA (fp32)
studies.note: GPU value proposition (see the Powerhouse scaling note): the CUDA GPU must buy speed over the fp64 CPU to justify its float32 precision, and it does -- materially faster than CPU at large n (up to ~15x for OLS and ~5-6x for the GLM families at n=5e5, p=128), narrowing toward parity at small n / narrow p where the CPU is preferable. The CPU stays the R-equivalent reference path (priority 3); the GPU is the throughput path and is held to actually delivering it. OLS + GLM device scaling, CPU (fp64) vs CUDA (fp32).

studies.title: GPU GLM stability at scale — Powerhouse (MPS): plain converges, ridge holds
studies.note: GPU GLM stability at scale (MPS). The plain (unpenalized) float32 log-link fit converges and ridge holds -- unchanged from 4.2.3. 4.2.4 changes the MPS float32 inner solve to a gated matrix-free conjugate gradient (squaring-free; host float64 acceptance gate unchanged), so the float32 solve no longer relies on a positive-definite float32 Cholesky, but the convergence outcomes on this grid are identical. fp64 is unsupported on MPS (no float64).

studies.title: GPU GLM stability at scale — Forge (CUDA): plain, ridge, and fp64
studies.note: GPU GLM stability at scale (CUDA). Plain float32 log-link now CONVERGES (~1e-6 vs CPU, was fail-loud at 3.20.0); ridge converges; gpu_fp64 is exact (~1e-15). The 4.2.3 fp32 stop-rule fix resolved the plain-log-link failure on CUDA as well as MPS.

studies.title: Hard-case correctness — behaviour match vs R (R10)
studies.note: Adversarial grid (RIGOR R10): pystatistics is checked against R's BEHAVIOUR, not just its coefficients. Logistic separation (complete + quasi) — both diverge and flag non-convergence (pystatistics via converged=False at the iteration cap; R via converged=False and the 'fitted probabilities numerically 0 or 1' warning). Factor + interaction contrast coding — pystatistics' own treatment-contrast term builder produces the identical model matrix to R's default contrasts (design bijection) and the identical fit. Rank-deficient/aliased designs — pystatistics drops the aliased column to NaN in the SAME position as R's NA. Prior weights and offsets are SUPPORTED as of 4.3.0 and validated here as correctness: weighted OLS matches R's lm(weights=) to round-off (coef/SE), an offset Poisson rate model matches R's glm(offset=) to round-off, and the GPU float32 path reproduces the CPU weighted/offset fit to the fp32 tier.

studies.title: Hard-case correctness — ill-conditioned / GPU refusal boundary (R10)
studies.note: Condition-number sweep (RIGOR R10). The CPU QR path agrees with R to round-off at EVERY conditioning (cpu_coef_max_rel_vs_r). The GPU fp32 Cholesky path is a true classifier: where it ACCEPTS, it matches the CPU fit in predictions (gpu_fitted_rel_vs_cpu) and residual sum of squares (gpu_rss_rel_vs_cpu) — the growing per-coefficient gap (gpu_coef_rel_vs_cpu) is the inherent non-identifiability of an ill-conditioned design in float32, NOT a wrong fit; the fit itself tracks CPU. Where float32 cannot represent the solve (the fp32-Gram condition gate exceeds 1e6, or the fp32 Cholesky loses positive-definiteness) it FAILS LOUD (gpu_status=refused), never a silently-wrong answer; force=True overrides the gate. The decision variable is the backend's own fp32-Gram condition (lib_cond_fp32), conservative relative to the true fp64 condition (np_cond); rows are sorted by it so the boundary reads monotonically.

studies.title: Precision-vs-hardware isolation — Forge (CUDA): gpu_fp64 vs cpu_fp64 (R11)
studies.note: GPU speedup attribution (RIGOR R11): the GPU exists to be faster than the CPU, but the headline GPU-vs-CPU number bundles two effects -- the float32-vs-float64 win and the GPU-vs-CPU hardware win. This study separates them so the speedup is honest and attributable, and confirms the gpu_fp64 path is numerically exact. speedup_fp32_vs_cpu is the BUNDLED headline (hardware + float32); speedup_fp64_vs_cpu is the same-precision, hardware-ONLY win (both float64). gpu_fp64 agrees with the CPU fit to ~1e-13..1e-15 (the numerically-exact path), so the isolated timing compares equivalent computation. The bundled GPU win is roughly half hardware, half precision at scale; at small n the fp64 GPU is slower than CPU (kernel/transfer overhead) — the hardware win emerges only at large n. CUDA only: Apple Silicon has no float64.

studies.title: Reference BLAS provenance (R11)
studies.note: Which BLAS each host's R linked against (RIGOR R11) — without it the CPU-vs-R gap is uninterpretable. Powerhouse R uses Apple Accelerate (a fast vendor BLAS); Forge R uses the reference (netlib) BLAS (single-threaded, unoptimised). The CPU-vs-R speedups in the correctness study are therefore against DIFFERENT R baselines: beating Accelerate-backed R (powerhouse) is the stronger result; the larger Forge margins partly reflect R's slow reference BLAS there.

studies.title: fp32 GPU GLM no-silent-wrong boundary — Powerhouse (MPS) (R12)
studies.note: Adversarial no-silent-wrong proof (RIGOR R12, the complement of R9) for the relaxed plain float32 log-link GLM, on the MPS gated matrix-free CG path. Designs straddle the float32 floor along three axes (near-collinear conditioning, large coefficients, heavy low-weight blocks — the discrete-time baseline-hazard pathology). For every ACCEPTED fit the deviance is compared to the float64 reference: accepted_dev_rel_vs_fp64 stays at the float32 tier (<=5e-7 here), i.e. the accepted fit reached the SAME optimum. For every REFUSED fit the fit is FORCED and checked against float64 (forced_dev_rel_vs_fp64): a true positive forces to a genuinely-wrong / overflowing fit, while 'refused-force-recovers' rows are a conservative gate where force=True still recovers a correct fit. NO row is classified SILENT-WRONG — the accept/refuse gate never accepts a wrong fit. (accepted_coef_rel can exceed the deviance tier on ill-conditioned designs: non-identifiable coefficients, not a wrong optimum — cf. the collinear OLS study.)

studies.title: fp32 GPU GLM no-silent-wrong boundary — Forge (CUDA) (R12)
studies.note: The same R12 no-silent-wrong proof on the CUDA Cholesky path. Every ACCEPTED float32 fit reached the float64 optimum (accepted_dev_rel_vs_fp64 <= ~1e-6); gpu_fp64 is exact vs CPU (fp64_dev_rel_vs_cpu ~ round-off). REFUSED fits are dominated by true positives (forced fit wrong/overflowing). NO row is SILENT-WRONG. The CUDA Cholesky and MPS gated-CG paths have DIFFERENT accept envelopes (CUDA accepts some large-coefficient designs MPS refuses, and vice versa) but share the same guarantee: never accept a wrong fit, never return a silently-wrong number.

studies.title: R12 (inference): SEs/CIs never silently understate instability — Powerhouse (MPS)
studies.note: Extends the R12 no-silent-wrong proof from the deviance/optimum to the INFERENCE outputs (the standard errors), which is the product's differentiator. R12 shows an accepted fit reaches the right optimum, but on a near-collinear design the coefficients become non-identifiable even there (coef_rel up to ~1). The decisive question is whether the reported fp32 SEs blow up to reflect that (a large SE warns the user, exactly as R does) or understate it (a coefficient wrong yet looking precise -- an inference-silent-wrong). Across OLS + log-link Poisson/Gamma over a conditioning sweep on MPS, EVERY accepted fp32 GPU fit is inference-warned: the SEs match the fp64 CPU fit to the documented Tier-2 contract (se_rel_gpu_vs_cpu <= 1e-2, here <= ~4e-4) and match R (the gamma rows carry the documented ~1e-2 dispersion-estimator gap), and the SE on the least-identified coefficient grows with conditioning (cpu_se_max/gpu_se_max track together from ~0.05 to ~160). NO accepted fit understates its SE. This is mathematically necessary -- the SE is sqrt(diag of the same (XtX)^-1 / (XtWX)^-1 that drives the instability, so a non-identifiable coefficient must carry a large SE -- and here it is confirmed empirically in float32.

studies.title: R12 (inference): SEs/CIs never silently understate instability — Forge (CUDA)
studies.note: The same inference-trustworthiness proof on the CUDA Cholesky path. CUDA's accept envelope reaches genuinely non-identifiable designs -- e.g. the OLS row at eq_cond ~ 6.7e4 is ACCEPTED with coef_rel ~ 0.998 (coefficients ~100% off) yet se_rel_gpu_vs_cpu ~ 1e-4 and its SE has blown up to ~158, matching CPU and R. EVERY accepted fp32 fit is inference-warned; NO row understates its SE. So even where the float32 coefficients are non-identifiable, the reported standard errors correctly flag them as untrustworthy -- the inference user gets the same warning they would from R, never a wrong coefficient that looks precise.

record_fields.coef_max_rel: max relative difference between pystatistics and R over the coefficient vector (correctness headline)
record_fields.se_max_rel: max relative difference over the standard-error vector
record_fields.speedup_vs_r: R wall-clock / pystatistics wall-clock on the same fit (>1 means pystatistics is faster)
record_fields.peak_mem_mb: peak memory during the fit (GPU allocator high-water mark; process RSS delta on CPU)
record_fields.plain_status: outcome of a plain GPU GLM fit at scale: converged or raised (fails loud when float32 is unreliable)
record_fields.ridge_status: outcome of a ridge GPU GLM fit (the penalty conditions the float32 solve)
record_fields.ridge_rel_vs_cpu_ridge: ||Δβ||/||β|| of the ridge GPU fit vs the CPU ridge fit (float32 tier)
record_fields.fp64_status: gpu_fp64 outcome — converged on CUDA, unsupported on MPS (no float64)
record_fields.fp64_rel_vs_cpu: ||Δβ||/||β|| of the gpu_fp64 fit vs the CPU fit (~1e-15, numerically exact)
